content:
Students in University College may have noticed posters on the walls for a new offshoot of the Black Hole Student Group. Theatre major Syd Burke-Davis has taken it into their own hands to form a new U of M Improv Club. They do not seem to have been the only one awaiting such an opportunity either — after their first two meetings, the Improv Club was reported to average 13 attendees dropping in throughout the session.

Each meeting includes warm-up exercises, theory, practices and games to teach a given skill for improvisational performance, such as building on others’ ideas and creating characters. For example, in one meeting, the participants played contestants on a dating panel show. In another game that same day, they were given superhero names to build characters around.

“The best way to learn anything is with a group of like-minded people who are just putting themselves out there, and the low stakes of it all is really important to getting yourself out of your own head and actually being in the space and taking in what people are giving you,” Burke-Davis explained. “I’m trying to create the impression that we’re all learning here. Even though we’re all at different skill levels, we all have something to improve on.”

Learning to improvise can help build everyday social skills as well.

“One of the very basic things in improv that you learn to do [is] listen to the people around you […] which helps in a conversation because anything that the person who you’re talking to says, you have to build off of that and show them that you were listening with your response,” Burke-Davis said. They were an active member of their high school’s improv club, which was their favourite part of attending the collegiate and where they made many friends. After a gap year, they came to the U of M eager to join a similar student group but disappointingly found no such thing. After waiting two years for one to begin, they took the initiative.

“[The club] has taught me that you don’t really need permission to get together with your fellow students and do something cool together,” they reflected. “There [are] systems in place to set up larger things, but if you just want to do small get-togethers, just set that up, just get connected, make a Telegram group chat and invite your friends to it. Take that initiative and see where it goes.”

The U of M Improv Club meets on Wednesdays from 12:30 to 2:20 p.m. at 145 University College, with a casual drop-in format.
